title: Two Lost Boutiques, a Refused Franchise and the First Kaldi's Café
dek: After city development closed her clothing shops, Tseday Asrat opened a Starbucks-style café in Addis Ababa and named it after Ethiopia's legendary goatherd.

story.event: Opening the first Kaldi's café in Addis Ababa after losing her clothing boutiques
story.summary: In about 2003 city development forced Tseday Asrat to close her two clothing boutiques in Addis Ababa; on her husband's suggestion she turned to coffee and, after Starbucks reportedly refused her a franchise, opened her own café, Kaldi's, in Bole Medhanialem in 2004. Its logo deliberately resembled Starbucks'. The chain grew to 30 company-owned cafés by 2016, and supply problems led her to set up her own coffee roastery and dairy.
paragraphs: In about 2003, Tseday Asrat was running two clothing boutiques in Addis Ababa. She had opened the first, Seasonal Style, at 23, selling imported clothes, and added a second about six months later against the advice of people close to her. After roughly two years both had to go: city development and expansion forced her out of the premises. She was pregnant with her second child, and it was her husband, Elias Ketema, an Ethiopian Airlines pilot, who suggested she move from clothes into coffee and start with a café.

She had no university degree; she had modelled from the age of 18 and worked briefly for a travel agency. What she had was a model she admired. According to a French reporter who visited in 2007, she asked Starbucks whether she could open a franchise in Ethiopia and was turned down. While reading the American chain's website, she later said, she came across the legend of Kaldi, the Ethiopian herdsman said to have discovered coffee, and took his name. Ethiopians make time in their day for coffee with colleagues and friends, she told another interviewer, and it is affordable.

In 2004 she opened the first Kaldi's in Bole Medhanialem. She later admitted the logo was meant to resemble Starbucks': "it was very important when we started the business," she said. In the early days, by her account, Elias cleaned the floors and toilets himself to set the standard for cleaning. Accounts of her ambition differ. She told one interviewer she had not even thought about a second café at first; Ethiopian Business Review recalled that she had spoken of forty, which many thought immodest.

About 18 months in, the number of customers persuaded her to open a second café, and others followed. Growth brought its own problems. When roasted coffee ran short in 2011 she began roasting her own, and because suppliers' milk was sometimes adulterated she built a dairy. Starbucks later challenged the logo; she said she won because the resemblance lay in colour and beans, which the law could not protect. By 2016 Kaldi's had 30 cafés, none of them franchised, and her businesses employed about 1,800 people.

quote.text: Even if there shall appear in you a likeness to him who, by reason of your admiration, has left a deep impress upon you, I would have you resemble him as a child resembles his father, and not as a picture resembles its original; for a picture is a lifeless thing.
quote.work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium)
quote.source_title: Moral letters to Lucilius, Letter 84, translated by Richard Mott Gummere (Loeb Classical Library, volume 2, 1920), Wikisource
quote.connection: Seneca allows a likeness to someone admired, provided it is a living one. Kaldi's logo was close to a picture of the original, and Asrat said she needed it to be; the roastery, the dairy and the staff she trained grew into something else. Both are true of the same company.

reflection: Very little starts from nothing. Tseday Asrat lost two shops she had built, borrowed an idea she admired, and then spent years on the unglamorous work that made it hers: roasting her own coffee, making her own milk, training waiters who later became managers.

You borrow too, from colleagues, from places you trained, from people whose work you respect. That is not a failing. The question worth asking now and then is which parts you have only copied and which you have taken in and changed. The copied parts are often what people notice first. The changed ones are usually what makes the work yours.
invitation: Pick one thing in your work that you took from someone you admire: a format, a habit, a way of explaining. Write one sentence on what you have changed about it, or would change if it were fully yours.

cross_checks.claim: Both of her clothing boutiques closed in about 2003 because city development forced her out of the premises
The first Kaldi's café opened in 2004 (in Bole Medhanialem)
She first sought a Starbucks franchise and, when that did not happen, started her own café named after Kaldi
Supply problems led her to roast her own coffee and set up her own dairy
By 2016 Kaldi's had about 30 cafés and her businesses employed about 1,800 people

research_notes: Founding year: Ethiopian Business Review (2016) dates the first branch, in Bole Medhanialem, to 2004; How we made it in Africa (2019) puts the boutique closures in 2003 and the first café 'a year later'; AWiB (September 2017) says 'thirteen years later', which also points to 2004; How we made it in Africa's 2015 interview says 'established in 2005'; Addis Fortune's report on the Dubai branch gives 2008, which conflicts with every other source and is not cited. The story uses 2004. Ambition: EBR's introduction says the controversy began because she said she would open 40 branches; in the 2015 interview she said she had not thought about more than one café at first. The story gives both and attributes each. Starbucks franchise: the refusal is reported by Afrik.com (2007); in EBR she says only that she first planned to franchise Starbucks, then found the Kaldi legend on its website. The story attributes the refusal to the French reporter. Logo dispute: only EBR reports Starbucks' later challenge, in the journalist's words and hers; Afrik.com in 2007 reported that Starbucks was said not to mind. The story gives the challenge in her account. Café counts rise across sources with date: more than 20 (2015), 30 (EBR, 2016), 33 (AWiB, 2017), 38 (2019); the story uses EBR's 2016 figure, with 1,800 employees across her enterprises (EBR) rather than for the cafés alone. Spelling: sources use both Tseday and Tsedey; the husband is 'Captain Elias' (AWiB) and 'Capitan Elias Ketema, an Ethiopian Airlines pilot' (EBR). Funding is set to unknown: no source says how the first café was paid for, although AWiB describes it as turning her boutique business into a coffee business. The Seneca passage is advice about imitating admired writers; it is applied here by analogy.
